title: Dealing with drunken guests and refusing service
siteNotes: Who the designated premises supervisor (DPS) is and how to reach them at any hour
Where the incident or refusals log is kept and how to fill it in
The premises licence conditions that apply here (for example door, capacity or last-orders rules)
Who to call first on a shift (duty manager) and the phone numbers
The venue's safe-ways-home options (local taxi firm numbers, rooms available, who may arrange a lift)
The venue's rule for a refused guest who insists on driving off: who decides to call the police.
legalNotes: Selling or attempting to sell alcohol to a person who is drunk, or allowing it to be sold to them, when done knowingly, is an offence under Licensing Act 2003 s.141. Verified on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2003/17/section/141. The section lists who can commit it (anyone authorised to sell, the premises licence holder, the DPS and others). Penalties deliberately not quoted: not verified.

Knowingly allowing disorderly conduct on licensed premises is an offence under s.140. Not verified word for word: the legislation page could not be retrieved in full, so the session describes it in general terms only.
Premises licence conditions vary by venue and are listed on the licence: your manager will show you.

Signs of drunkenness, the refuse-the-drink approach, water, food, safe ways home and when to call 999 are good practice, not statute. The 'no physical contact unless needed for safety' point is general good practice and not tied to one regulation.

Mandatory licensing conditions (free tap water on request, and responsible promotions) are in the Licensing Act 2003 (Mandatory Licensing Conditions) Order 2010, legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2010/860. Verified.
Drinks spiking is a crime. A specific offence or section was not verified and is not quoted. Advice to report to the police is good practice.
Not verified: any fine or time limit for s.140 or s.141, and the BBPA/gov.uk wording on drunkenness. Flagged for the GM.

Review 6 Oct 2026: s.141 text re-read on legislation.gov.uk. Offence is knowingly selling or attempting to sell alcohol to a drunk person, or knowingly allowing such a sale, on relevant premises; it applies to a person working at the premises in a capacity (paid or unpaid) that authorises them to prevent the sale, the premises licence holder and the DPS (and club officers or temporary event users in those settings). Penalty on summary conviction is a fine up to level 3; not quoted in the session. Only change: the why-text of the check about the guest who shouts after refusal now says serving someone you know is drunk is an offence, rather than that giving in 'breaks the law' (the offence needs knowledge).

Refused guest who says they will drive: staff cannot lawfully stop a guest driving or take their keys; the session correctly says to tell a manager, offer a taxi or lift, and not to use physical contact. When the police are called is a venue decision (siteNotes).

cards.kicker: Front of house, bar and events · 14 minutes
cards.title: Dealing with drunken guests and refusing service
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why we must not serve someone who is drunk
- spot the signs and refuse service calmly
- know when to get a manager, or call 999

cards.title: Why we do not serve drunk guests
cards.body:
It is an offence to knowingly sell alcohol to someone who is drunk, or to allow it to be sold to them. That is section 141 of the Licensing Act 2003.

It can fall on the person who serves, the licence holder and the designated premises supervisor. Your manager will show you who that is here.

> Refusing is you doing your job properly, not being rude.

items.label: Section 141: knowingly selling to a drunk person
Who can be liable: server, licence holder, DPS

cards.title: Signs someone has had enough
cards.body:
No single sign proves it. Look at the whole picture, and compare with how the guest was when they arrived.

If you are unsure, do not guess alone. Ask a colleague or your manager.

items.title: Behaviour
items.text: Aggressive, over-friendly or can't follow a conversation

cards.title: Refuse the drink, not the person
cards.body:
Keep it short, private and calm. Say what you cannot do, not what is wrong with them.

> "I'm sorry, I can't serve you another drink tonight. Can I get you a water or something to eat?"

Do not argue, joke at their expense or make it public.

items.title: Step away
items.text: Speak quietly, away from the crowd

items.title: Offer
items.text: Water, food, a seat, a taxi

items.title: Hold firm
items.text: Do not give in if they push

cards.title: Calm words, no contact
cards.body: Stay at an arm's length or more. Do not touch the guest unless it is needed to keep someone safe. If a guest will not accept a refusal, tell a manager.

left.title: Do
items: Make sure colleagues back the refusal

right.title: Do not
items: Let them be served by a colleague

cards.title: Keeping them safe afterwards
cards.body:
A refused guest is still our responsibility until they are safe. Ask if someone can collect them, offer to call a taxi, or tell a manager if they are staying in a room. Never let them drive.

Your manager will show you the venue's taxi and lift arrangements.

items.title: Call your manager
items.text: If they won't leave or are refusing help

items.title: Call 999
items.text: Unconscious, injured, violent or in danger

cards.title: When it is an emergency
cards.body:
Call 999 straight away if someone cannot be woken, is vomiting while drowsy, is injured, or someone is being hurt or threatened.

Leave the guest in the recovery position if you are trained and it is safe, and stay with them until help arrives. Do not wait for a manager first.

cards.title: Spotting a spiked drink
cards.body:
Spiking is a crime. A guest who suddenly seems far more drunk than their drinks explain, or is very drowsy or confused, may have been spiked.

✔ Stay with them and keep them with friends
✔ Tell a manager at once
✔ Call 999 if they are very unwell
✘ Do not let them leave alone or go off with a stranger

items.title: Sudden effects
items.text: Drowsy, confused, sick after few drinks

cards.title: Write it down
cards.body:
After any refusal or incident, tell your manager and record it: the time, what happened, who was involved and what you did. Do it while you remember it well.

Your manager will show you where the log is kept.

Stick to facts, not opinions.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Never knowingly serve someone who is drunk: it is an offence.
- Refuse the drink, not the person. Stay calm and private.
- Offer water and food, and make sure they get home safely.
- No contact unless needed for safety. Get a manager; call 999 if it is an emergency.
- Write it down.

cards.q: A guest is slurring and swaying and asks for another pint. A friend says, 'he's fine, I'll drink it.' What do you do?
options: Serve it, as the friend is taking responsibility
Refuse politely and offer water or food
Serve a half instead
Ask him to prove he can walk straight
cards.why: Once someone is drunk we do not serve them, whoever says they will drink it. Refuse calmly and offer water or food.

cards.q: Under section 141 only the licence holder can be guilty of knowingly selling to a drunk person.
cards.why: The offence can also apply to the person who serves and to the designated premises supervisor, not just the licence holder.

cards.q: After you refuse a guest, he gets louder and starts shouting at you at the bar. What is best?
options: Shout back so others hear your reason
Hold his arm and walk him to the door
Stay calm, keep your distance and fetch a manager
Serve him to settle him down
cards.why: Keep your voice low, do not touch him and get your manager. Serving someone you know is drunk is an offence, and physical contact can make things worse.

cards.q: Which TWO of these mean you should call 999 straight away?
options: A guest is loud and singing
A guest cannot be woken
A guest wants a taxi
A guest is being threatened or assaulted
A guest is unsteady on the stairs
cards.why: Someone who cannot be woken, or anyone in danger of being hurt, needs the emergency services without delay.

cards.q: A guest who has had two drinks becomes suddenly drowsy and confused. They may have been spiked, so a manager should be told at once.
cards.why: Effects that are far stronger than expected can mean spiking. Stay with them, tell a manager and call 999 if they are very unwell.

cards.q: Which of these is the best clue that a guest may be drunk?
options: He has ordered three pints in an hour
He is slurring, swaying and spilling his drink
He is chatty and laughing with friends
He has asked where the toilets are
cards.why: Look at speech, movement and behaviour together, compared with how they were when they arrived. Chat or laughter alone proves nothing.

cards.q: If a drunk guest has been refused, it is fine for a colleague to serve them a half instead.
cards.why: A refusal stands for the whole team. Serving them anyway risks the same offence, so tell colleagues about the refusal.

cards.q: A refused guest says he will drive home. What do you do?
options: Wish him goodnight, as it is his own choice to make
Tell a manager and offer a taxi or sober lift
Take his keys from his pocket to stop him
Tell him to wait ten minutes and then go
cards.why: Never let a drunk guest drive. Offer a safe way home and tell a manager. Taking keys is physical contact and is not your place.

cards.q: After refusing a guest, you only need to record it if the guest becomes aggressive.
cards.why: Record any refusal or incident while you remember it: time, what happened, what you did and who you told.

cards.q: A guest has been refused and is calm but sits swaying at the bar. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore him and let him leave in his own time
Offer water and food and tell a manager
Ask him to wait outside on the pavement
Stand over him until he finally leaves
cards.why: Offering water and food and involving a manager keeps him safe and calm. Leaving him alone, or crowding him, does not.
